skill.name: Hyperbole
skill.why: Writers stretch the truth on purpose to make a feeling big, or funny.
skill.how: Find the part that can't be true. Ask what it really means, and why.

beats.say: Sometimes writers stretch the truth on purpose.
beats.show: My school bag weighs **a thousand kilos**.

beats.say: Could a school bag really weigh that much? No way!
A big stretch like that is called hyperbole.
It makes a feeling bigger, and often funnier. Like my jokes.

weDo.text: Mo dropped his bag on the deck. 'This thing weighs more than the whole boat,' he groaned. 'I've been carrying it for a hundred years.' Gus peeked inside. There were six cans of beans and a pineapple.
weDo.hint: Could a bag really weigh more than a boat? So what is Mo really saying?
weDo.success: His bag is really heavy. Mo stretches the truth to show how tired he is of carrying it.

His bag weighs more than the boat.
options.reason: A bag of beans can't weigh more than a boat. Mo is stretching the truth.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote a letter to the island ranger. A Whopskip is peeking over her shoulder.
encounters.text:
Dear Ranger Tan,

This morning I found a pelican tangled in fishing line near the boardwalk. Its wing was caught, and it couldn't fly. I phoned your office at eight o'clock. Then I waited forever for you to come. I sat on the boardwalk, talking quietly to the pelican so it would stay calm. The mosquitoes ate me alive. When you arrived just before ten, you cut the line in about two seconds. The pelican flapped once, looked at us, and flew off. Thank you for coming in the end, even if my legs are now one big itchy bump.

Wren

encounters.frame: Gus has left his lab diary open on the galley table. The Whopskip is holding its nose.
encounters.text: Lab diary, Day 34. The Stink Sock is ready. I have worn this sock for five weeks without washing it, including three footy games and one very sweaty bushwalk. Today I opened the jar for the first time. The smell could melt the paint off a battleship. Mo, who was standing two metres away, sat down on the deck without a word. A seagull flying overhead turned around and went back the way it came. Zed said his eyebrows were trying to leave his face. I have put the lid back on and wrapped the jar in three plastic bags. I wrote down every reaction in my notebook, with times. At 9.02, Mo sat down. At 9.03, the seagull left. At 9.05, Wren opened every porthole on the boat and asked me, very politely, never to do that again. Next step: test it on Maxx's guards. That's not gross. That's science.

encounters.frame: Mo wrote Gus an apology letter. Tully summed it up, but got one word wrong.
encounters.text:
Dear Gus,

I am writing to say sorry about your slime experiment. I know you have been working on it since roughly the beginning of time, and I know it was meant to win the Island Science Fair. When I saw the bucket of green goo in the galley, I honestly thought it was lime jelly. I was so hungry that I could have eaten the entire boat, including the anchor, so I grabbed a spoon.

I only had one mouthful. It tasted like a swimming pool full of old socks. I have brushed my teeth four hundred times since then, and my tongue is still green. I am so sorry that I will probably never sleep again.

To make it up to you, I have bought you a new bucket and three bottles of glue, and I will clean the galley every night for a week. I have also written a sign for the bucket that says NOT JELLY in capital letters. Please forgive me. You are my best mate in the whole history of the universe.

Mo

encounters.frame: Zed posted about Swamp Dash Level 50 on the crew chat. The Whopskip helped, by sitting on the controller.
encounters.text: Crew, I have finally beaten Level 50 of Swamp Dash, and I need to tell you about it. First of all, the final boss, a giant robot crocodile, had about nine billion health points, and every jump needed perfect timing, down to a millionth of a second. I'm fairly sure I started this level back in Year 2. While I was waiting for the last checkpoint to load, my apple went mouldy and then turned into soil. Gus brought me a sandwich when I started, and by the time I finished, he had grown a long grey beard. When I finally landed the last hit, I cheered so loudly that the street lights in the whole town flickered, and the controller buzzed loud enough to wake every sleeping baby in Victoria. For the record, the level has twelve checkpoints, three hidden keys and a lava bridge that collapses if you stand still. I found two keys on my own and the third with a guide. Tully says I owe her a new pair of earmuffs. Now I'm going to lie down for about a decade.

encounters.frame: The Mirage Mangroves surf club pinned up this report. The Whopskip can't swim in surf, so it's just reading.
encounters.text:
SURF REPORT: OUTER BAR, SATURDAY. A strong southerly swell arrived overnight, and by seven o'clock the waves on the outer bar had reached about three metres, measured from the club tower. Sets were rolling in every eleven seconds, with a nasty rip running out beside the rocks at the northern end. The water temperature had dropped to sixteen degrees, so most surfers wore full wetsuits and booties.

Only the most experienced club members paddled out, and not a single surfer caught a wave before nine, because the sets were breaking so fast and so close together. At around ten, club veteran Bev Nguyen caught the wave of the morning. From the top of it, she could have waved to the passengers on passing planes, and she rode it all the way to the sand without falling off once. The crowd on the beach cheered and blew their whistles.

By lunchtime, the wind had swung round to the north-east and the swell was easing. The red and yellow flags are back up, and the club barbecue starts at two.

encounters.frame: A page from a young astronaut's training diary has washed up in the mangroves.
encounters.text:
Training diary, Week 12. Today was the day I'd been dreading since I first signed up: the spinning chair. It's a seat on the end of a long metal arm that whirls you round and round to test how much your body can take before you black out or throw up. The instructor strapped me in and gave me a paper bag, which did not make me feel any better.

The moment the arm started to turn, my stomach dropped about forty floors. After one minute, my cheeks were pulled back so far that I could see my own ears. After two minutes, I'm fairly sure my brain had swapped places with my lunch. The instructor's voice came through the headset, calm and slow, telling me to breathe, but I couldn't remember how breathing worked. Six minutes felt like six hundred years.

When the arm finally stopped, I sat there with my eyes shut while the room kept spinning without me. I didn't need the paper bag, which my instructor said makes me one of only three trainees this year. Tomorrow I have to do it again. I am going to eat a very small breakfast.

encounters.success: Seeing your own ears and swapped brains stretch how awful the spinning felt, so the writer was struggling badly.
